📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire.
  • British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
  • It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that its students should pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a last minute concession to get the deal over the line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire.

UK-EU summit live – latest news updates.

British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.

It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that its students should pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a last minute concession to get the deal over the line.

The UK had strongly resisted EU text on the table committing it to home fees instead of “significantly reduced” international fees, but a compromise was hammered out before 10pm, with a “supplementary agreement” to work out the details within the next six months.

Brussels insiders said the EU had kicked the can down the road and agreed not to mention the tuition fees rate in the declaration, with further negotiations to follow in the next six months.

As talks went into the night, EU sources suggested both sides were on track for an agreement within the next day.

According to recent reports, on Friday morning, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, stated the UK and Europe were “stronger together”, adding: “The test for this summit is simple: does it make life better for people in Britain? That is what I will deliver in Brussels today – cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people.”.

The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the BBC that Burnham’s approach amounted to a “betrayal”. He noted: “He’s trying to do it incrementally but it’s perfectly clear that this very very soon becomes a debate about do we rejoin or do we stay out.”.

But he acknowledged that for food exporters a deal on agricultural standards would make things “a little bit easier”.

On the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source mentioned.

There also seemed to be a compromise by France after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.

According to recent reports, the UK had demanded a “voting” role on some law-making in relation to food standards but France heavily opposed, and London eventually conceded on a point many think was unrealistic from the start. Instead, the UK will be consulted on latest food laws, but the details on the level of involvement remain to be seen.

Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a fresh youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.

It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year.

With less than 24 hours to go before Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some sticking points.

Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, another EU diplomat remarked: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”.

A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.

At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4% to British GDP, including the highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.

The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.

Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 remarked the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting upcoming SPS rules. An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”.

Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.

A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position mentioned the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.

It has been revealed that in contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK. “Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.

It has been revealed that the issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” remarked a second EU diplomat.

The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.

The concern raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state. The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.

Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was a UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.

“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We've closed the blog. Below is a roundup of the biggest headlines from Germany on Thursday, November 19.

It has been revealed that we're closing the blog today after a busy day in Berlin. We'll be back tomorrow with the latest headlines. Tschüss!

European powers rallied behind Ukraine at a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin earlier today.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz emphasized that he wanted European powers to play a role in bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.

"We know that this war will only end if there is a diplomatic solution," Merz stated after the meeting in the German capital on Thursday.

"But this war must end with a Ukraine that preserves its territorial integrity, has strong security guarantees on its side and is above all embedded in European security," he added.

Find out everything that happened here and here.

In a recent development, IG Metall, Germany's largest union, railed against automaker Volkswagen's latest demands on its workforce days before both sides are set to begin collective bargaining talks next Tuesday. The union described VW's vision for the future of work at the Wolfsburg-based giant as a "catalog of horrors.".

Recent findings suggest that VW, the world's second-largest car company by both sales and production, has seen profits nosedive — it declared quarterly losses of €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) in October — for a number of reasons, ranging from increased competition to tariffs and soft sales. Now the company plans to slash 120,000 jobs at 10 brands by 2030.

Arguing that its financial outlook has "deteriorated," VW management says it has no choice but to make deeper cuts faster than expected.

It has been revealed that VW wants to scrap the current contract's 35-hour week and is demanding employees work overtime without pay if needed and went so far as to announce that pay would be "adjusted" if workers were forced to work fewer than 35 hours. Moreover, it is calling for a pay freeze for 2027-2028, as well as cuts to benefits for long-term employees.

IG Metall notes workers haven't seen a raise since May 2024 and is calling for a 5% hike now, citing ever-rising living costs.

Regional IG representative Thorsten Gröger noted, "VW management is stabbing its employees the back." He added that negotiations will be "tenacious, bitter and exhausting" and that they "will leave deep scars at the firm.".

Workers are primed for walkouts, with the union warning that the battle may be far larger than anything VW has ever seen.

VW works council chairwoman Daniela Cavallo, who represents employees within the company, remarked, "Management's promises are obviously worthless." Cavallo said workers felt "betrayed" after they agreed to major job cuts for the health of the company two years ago.

The current contract applies to some 130,000 employees at German production sites in Braunschweig, Chemnitz, Dresden, Emden, Hanover, Kassel, Salzgitter, Wolfsburg and Zwickau.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Thursday called on Europeans to be vigilant against far-right extremism and warned of divisions and labels in society.

Speaking during a visit to Auschwitz-Birkenau, a former concentration camp, Pistorius noted the site bore witness to the worst of Nazi Germany's crimes, calling it an absolute low point.

"It all started with defining what made a life unworthy; by dividing according to race, origin, faith, sexual orientation," Pistorius warned, saying that such marginalization was experiencing a "renaissance" and "gaining ground with far-right extremist parties across Europe.".

The defense minister remarked Auschwitz provides all people, but particularly Germans, with a "symbol warning that we all bear responsibility for what happens and what must not be allowed to happen.".

During his tour of the camp, Pistorius laid a wreath at its death wall, where Nazi soldiers shot roughly 5,000 prisoners dead, and lit a candle at the victims' memorial.

Before he departed the site, Pistorius expressed his wish that more German students and travel groups would visit the camp "than appears to be the case at present.".

The deputy chairman of Germany's right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) has accused French presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen of deserting her core values in her bid to achieve wider popularity and improve her chance of victory in French presidential elections.

For years, Le Pen claimed to be embarking on a policy of what's often called "de-demonization," trying to shed the extreme-right image of her father and predecessor, Jean-Marie Le Pen, and soften the stance of the party now called the National Rally or RN.

"Mrs. Le Pen, whom we all once admired greatly, now seems to have one fundamental principle: I say whatever the polls demand of me," Sven Tristschler told the right-leaning website The Pioneer.

France is headed into the last months of a presidential election campaign, with incumbent Emmanuel Macron's second and final term coming to an end and no clear candidate emerging as a main challenger to Le Pen as yet.

Industry observers note that "At the end of the day, her victory would likely be even more catastrophic for the right than her defeat," Tritscher asserted. "The citizens would think they were voting to the right, only to get another Macron in the end.".

He said that in hindsight, he was glad the AfD and RN parties had fallen out in European politics in recent years, and said AfD supporters should not anticipate a similar move toward moderation.

"A hollowing-out will not take place with us," he said, using the German scientific term for enucleation, the removal of the internal nucleus or core of a cell.

The AfD has made similar complaints about Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, accusing her party of a process of "Melonization" involving a softening of its core policy stances in a bid to retain power.

A similar power struggle is thought to be brewing within the AfD itself as it remains far adrift of majority support despite regularly polling as the largest single party in Germany at present.

Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, remarked in its monthly report that inflation in Germany will rise "sharply" at the beginning of 2027.

Inflation could remain stable through the end of the year, given that a fuel tax cut is still keeping a lid on prices.

Inflation had fallen to 2.9% from 3.3% in September after the German government introduced the fuel discount.

But the central bank said the expiration of that fuel tax cut, along with other government measures, would drive inflation higher.

The report also highlighted that natural gas prices are expected to rise.

"On top of this, higher energy and input costs are expected to gradually feed through into the prices of other goods and certain services," the Bundesbank remarked.

German telecommunications firm, Deutsche Telekom, confirmed that it will invest €100 million ($109.75 million) in French start-up Mistral AI, Europe's largest artificial intelligence company.

The investment will pour into Mistral from Telekom's subsidiary T.Capital Tech Fund.

Telekom said the move is a first step toward a strategic partnership, where the two firms plan to jointly support companies and the public sector in Germany in introducing tailored AI.

"Europe’s competitiveness depends on our ability to develop and use powerful AI," Telekom board member Ferri Abolhassan remarked in a statement announcing the deal. "Businesses must be able to trust this technology while retaining control over their data.".

Recent findings suggest that the move is the latest investment by Telekom in the AI space. In February, Telekom built an AI factory in Munich, which has since been expanded due to high demand.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Berlin for a summit of the "Coalition of the Willing." The group, which represents Kyiv's allies, is expected to push for a deeper European role in any efforts to end the war.

The process has so far been dominated by the US, Russia and Ukraine.

Zelenskyy wrote on X that "we are doing everything we can to ensure that Europe's presence in the negotiation process is fully represented.".

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff flew to Germany to attend the summit at the Chancellery.

An 18-year-old in western Germany has been held in pre-trial detention in Germany since August over the alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack on a mosque, prosecutors have remarked.

The teen, who is from the town of Eslohe in North Rhine-Westphalia, allegedly held far-right extremist views and was planning the attack for late 2026 or early 2027, senior public prosecutor Alexandra Wiese said.

"He also directed his racist ideology against people of the Muslim faith," Wiese told public broadcaster WDR.

A search of the suspect's home led investigators to find numerous weapons, weapon parts and ammunition, including items manufactured using a 3D printer.

Wiese did not provide details of potential targets in order to protect possible victims.

No charges have yet been filed against the teen and Wiese stressed that the presumption of innocence applies as the investigation continues.

Italian commercial bank UniCredit and the German government reached agreement on the big sticking points of its takeover of Commerzbank.

The EU greenlit UniCredit's takeover of Germany's Commerzbank earlier this week.

The merging of ​UniCredit and Commerzbank would create a bank with more than €1.3 trillion ($1.4 trillion) in assets across two of the eurozone's largest economies.

It would be one of the most significant cross-border ​European banking deals in years.

In a statement to Reuters news agency, Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil mentioned Germany "supports a swift process and an orderly transition of control.".

"We have reached common ground and UniCredit has ‌made clear commitments to Germany as a business location, to the rights of Commerzbank employees and to a continued constructive dialogue with ‌the works ​council," Klingbeil noted, referring to a body of elected employee representatives.

Among the concessions, Germany is said to have given up its insistence on naming two supervisory board members to Commerzbank.

Meanwhile, UniCredit agreed to the key German demand to keep UniCredit's enlarged German business headquartered and listed in Frankfurt.

UniCredit also reportedly pledged to put German nationals on UniCredit's board of directors.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will travel to Poland for a two-day visit.

Pistorius is scheduled to meet his Polish counterpart, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, in the capital, Warsaw, for talks on defense policy.

Poland is a member of both the EU and NATO and is one of the most notable political and military allies of Ukraine.

The trip to Germany's neighbor to the east will begin with a stop at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was built during the German occupation of Poland during World War II.

Auschwitz-Birkenau is one of the biggest symbols of the Holocaust and Germany's Nazi regime, with some 1.1 million people having died in the camp between 1940 and 1945, most of them Jews.

The camp's victims were shot, murdered in gas chambers or died of starvation and disease.

The German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) stated in a report that cheap gadgets such as streaming boxes are increasingly being hijacked by cybercriminals.

According to the report, the number of hacked systems has nearly doubled within a year, with BSI reporting some 75,400 infected systems in Germany to internet providers every day, an 89% increase. Some of the gadgets were found to be already infected at the factory, the report says.

The vast majority of cases involved Android devices, particularly consumer electronics connected to the so-called "Internet of Things.".

BSI said criminals rent the hijacked devices as proxy botnets on the dark web to hide their own attacks, which would allow for consumers themselves to unknowingly come under investigators' scrutiny.

BSI President Claudia Plattner has also warned of AI-driven attacks.

"The disruption coming in particular from high-performance, agentic AI has set newly introduced benchmarks," she mentioned.

  • A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.
  • The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (Â£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US is playing catch-up with China's dominance in critical minerals mining and processing across Africa (file photo).

A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.

The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (Â£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.

Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".

The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.

Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.

Recent findings suggest that A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Barnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.

Recent findings suggest that mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.

The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.

There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.

Barnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance.".

The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.

The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders.

Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline.

Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.

The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.

Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.

Kenya's mining ministry notes the sector is an crucial part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

Latest Update: This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote.
  • In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort.
  • His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.

His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”.

In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.

In a recent development, “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” indicates Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”.

Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”.

Recent findings suggest that as a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.

Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.

According to recent reports, when Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.

Recent findings suggest that around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, newly introduced defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.

“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he notes.

To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch.

Sources indicate that in April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US.

Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” says Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.”.

It has been revealed that seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he indicates. “No one had ever seen that before.”.

When the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he said.

According to recent reports, the week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” states Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.”.

Sources indicate that by the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems.

Industry observers note that YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” states Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.”.

Dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes.

“You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” says Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.”.

But Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Major picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” claims Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”.

Industry observers note that so far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile.

Industry observers note that if he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these upcoming missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life?

In a recent development, dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these issues. He says he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies.

Industry observers note that by his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global problem. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he claims. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.”.

But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people.

Recent findings suggest that mcKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, debuted a drone startup in his early twenties. Initially, he had meant for the drones to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile manufacturer invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too. He left around the same time.

In a recent development, “I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” he says. “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an problem with it or he won’t.”.

In a recent development, polemos Industries declared itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video. Set to the ticking of a clock, it featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens.

The video climbed to the top of the trending page on X. In the responses, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first company. “Coming for him,” Dandzbergs responded.

It has been revealed that dandzbergs recognizes that people are likely to dismiss him for his age. But he considers youth one of his biggest advantages. “Please don’t say I’m sacrificing my childhood,” he indicates. “This is the childhood I dreamed of.”.

Valve has worked through the waitlist for the smaller version of its gaming PC.

Sources indicate that valve has announced that it's completed all of the waitlist orders for the smaller 512GB model of the Steam Machine and is now letting anyone buy it while supplies last. The change should make the experience of buying the Linux gaming PC a bit closer to the consoles it competes with, though Valve's announcement doesn't suggest dealing with RAMaggedon has gotten any easier.

According to recent reports, it's not clear how many 512GB Steam Machines are available, but rather than set up another waitlist, the tech giant states it will mark the model as "out of stock" once it sells through its current supply. Things are a bit more complicated for the 2TB model. Valve has "finished getting purchase invites out to all reservation holders" and anyone who joined the waitlist later will be able to keep their place in line. Because there are more people on the waitlist than units available to buy, though, Valve is closing the list to fresh sign-ups and marking the 2TB model as out of stock on Steam.

In a recent development, the organization claims Steam Machines will still be made, but it sounds like availability will fluctuate and the price could change. "We don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them," Valve says in its announcement. "The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.".

Sources indicate that the manufacturer originally instituted a waitlist as a way to manage interest in the Steam Machine after the Steam Controller became difficult to buy due to high demand. Valve has also been constrained by the current price of memory and storage, which has been driven up by the data center buildout powering the AI industry. Launching the Steam Machine for $1,049 was never Valve's blueprint, but a high price and limited supply appear to have tied the company's hands. Valve claims it expects to have more to share about Steam Machine availability in January.

Today's NYT Strands hints will be easy if you're always in a pickle.

Recent findings suggest that strands, the Latest York Times' elevated word-search game, requires the player to perform a twist on the classic word search. Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

Peter Walker and Jennifer Rankin.

With Andy Burnham arriving soon at the UK-EU summit the position is – well, much as it was last night, with a broad agreement but the most tricky problem kicked down the road for six months.

The official mood music from EU officials on Friday morning was positive, with talk of “concrete deliverables” for citizens on both sides in the three key areas: a deal on food and drink imports and exports; emissions trading; and the planned mutual “youth experience” exchange scheme.

“We expect the leaders to confirm and unlock the conclusion of three important negotiations that have been ongoing.”.

It has been revealed that there is, however, one snag remaining: no agreement on whether EU students coming to the UK to study should pay lower tuition fees than at the moment, and ideally for Brussels, the domestic rate. This aspect is subject to six more months of negotiations, and none of the other deals will be completed until this is also done.

While EU officials are not explicit about this, the assumption is that they are seeking UK tuition fee levels. This would, for Burnham and his ministers, be a tricky sell, especially to the university sector, who currently get fees several times higher than the UK rate for EU students.

For now, there is something of an impasse.

“I think our position has been clear. We think this is an issue that needs to be addressed,” one EU official noted.

Susan Smith's ex-husband makes emotional appeal against granting parole.

A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago has been denied parole for a second time.

Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and rolling her vehicle into a lake in 1994.

"I got to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake," Smith stated during a hearing on Thursday with the state board that decides whether to release those in prison on parole.

According to recent reports, the seven-member board later unanimously turned down her request to be freed. The father of the two boys has vowed to continue to oppose her release, and several people spoke against her in the hearing.

Smith, whose lawyers had argued she suffered a mental breakdown during the crime, can apply to the South Carolina Board of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services for parole every two years.

She told the board that she had changed and matured since killing three-year-old Michael and one-year-old Alex, and that "I am not the same person I was 32 years ago".

She also said she was "very, very sorry" and that she would go back and change the circumstances if she could.

Sources indicate that "They were innocent children," Smith mentioned. "They did not deserve to die.".

Her children's father, David Smith, attended the hearing so he could advocate for their sons, he said.

The 32 years, he said, do not take away what Smith "deliberately" did.

"I know in my heart granting her parole would be a huge injustice to Michael and Alex," said David Smith, who had pinned a photo of both his sons to his lapel.

Smith was convicted of killing her two sons in 1994.

Prosecutors argued during the trial that Smith killed the boys after a man with whom she was having an affair told her that her sons were the reason that the pair did not have a future together.

At Thursday's hearing, Smith noted: "This did not happen because of a man. That's just not true.".

When the boys first disappeared, Smith stated she was carjacked late at night and a man drove away with her car. While she pleaded publicly for their safe return, her sons were at the bottom of a nearby lake.

But ultimately she confessed to the crime.

Defence lawyers said she had wanted to die with her children but left the car at the last minute.

Smith was convicted of murder. Under South Carolina law at the time, she was allowed to request parole every two years after serving 30 years in prison.

In the US, some people convicted of crimes are eligible for parole, which means they can be released from incarceration.

She would have needed two-thirds of the board members present to vote in her favour to be freed.

Susan Smith denied parole 30 years after drowning her two sons.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, on the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War update.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Ukrainian barrage of missiles and drones collapsed a crucial segment of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Strait Bridge—and Ukraine’s military pulled off the strike deep within Russian-occupied territory without relying on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications to guide the missiles in.

According to recent reports, on the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War update. Russian sources claimed several hundred Ukrainian drones first overwhelmed Russian air defenses to pave the way for remote-controlled missile strikes focused on the bridge, with the latter prominently including Ukraine’s homegrown Flamingo cruise missile.

In a recent development, the Ukrainian operation adapted a Russian battlefield innovation by using drones equipped with mesh radios to create an airborne communications network, according to the Financial Times. Each networked drone acts as a relay node to extend the communication link between human operators and remotely piloted missiles and strike drones. Russia began using the technique to support long-range drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian cities.

During the Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Strait Bridge, the flying mesh network allowed operators located more than 250 kilometers away (155 miles) to remotely guide missiles and drones in evading Russian air defenses while also homing in on the bridge’s weakest structural points, according to the Financial Times.

Recent findings suggest that ukraine’s takedown of the bridge segment was preceded by weeks of preparatory strikes that systematically destroyed or degraded Russian air defense weapons, radars, and electronic warfare equipment arrayed to protect the bridge. The November 15 night attack on the bridge also coincided with the largest Ukrainian overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of the full-scale war, Reuters reported.

Notably, Ukraine conducted the coordinated strike with primarily Ukrainian developed or adapted technologies. The Financial Times reported that “Ukrainian units involved in the operation deliberately avoided using Starshield, the military version of Musk’s Starlink satellite network,” because of recent US restrictions that prevent Ukraine from using Starshield on drones or anything else traveling more than 100 miles per hour (161 kilometers per hour).

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that the latest US-imposed restrictions on Starshield have not yet been lifted, although SpaceX denied that the restrictions had returned. Zelenskyy described the speed limit as interfering with some Ukrainian drone interceptor technologies that were designed to defend against Russian drones attacking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.

However, the Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Strait Bridge provide yet another example of how the Ukrainian military and defense technology companies have been learning to fight without relying on Starlink. This is also not the first time that Ukraine, arguably the leading country in developing newly introduced battlefield uses of drones, has adopted a Russian battlefield innovation for its own uses.

Recent findings suggest that from Russia’s view, the only glimmer of good news was that the bridge’s railway section survived the initial strikes. Ukrainian newspaper the Kyiv Independent pointed to Russian news and video sources indicating that trains appeared to be running again on the bridge on November 18.

According to recent reports, but Ukraine targeted the railway section yet again in a follow-up strike on the night of November 18. Ukraine’s General Staff described having used Neptune cruise missiles operated by the Ukrainian Navy, and Russia-aligned officials in Crimea confirmed they had “temporarily suspended” train traffic on the bridge to assess the damage, ABC News reported.

Meanwhile, the severe damage to the bridge’s arch and roadway section cuts off a crucial transportation and supply link between Russia and the Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula of Ukraine. The Institute for the Study of War assesses that the “destruction of the bridge” will complicate Russia’s ability to maintain its occupation and military basing within the peninsula.

The other overland supply route between Russia and Crimea involves highways running through Russian-occupied southern Ukraine. But Ukrainian forces have already been striking such highway infrastructure and the Russian supply trucks running along the exposed route.

Fallen debris from the bridge’s collapsed arch may also prevent any large ship traffic from passing through the Kerch Strait that connects the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, according to a Telegram channel owner based in Crimea. That makes it even more difficult for Russia to resupply the Crimean Peninsula by sea—and Ukrainian drones have previously struck dozens of Russian ships in the Sea of Azov.

Beyond the physical damage to the bridge, such attacks represent a symbolic blow to Putin’s ambition of holding onto the Crimean Peninsula. After Russian forces seized Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, Russia based much of its Black Sea Fleet at the naval base in Sevastopol and later used the peninsula as a logistics hub for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Industry observers note that the $3.5 billion Kerch Strait Bridge was built as a physical link to cement Russia’s claim over Crimea. Putin personally drove a construction truck across the bridge to commemorate its opening in 2018. He repeated the bridge-crossing feat in a Mercedes in December 2022, after a Ukrainian truck bomb attack temporarily damaged the bridge in October of that year.

It has been revealed that in 2025, the bridge was damaged again after Ukraine’s Security Service used agents to plant mines under the bridge supports. Again, Russia repaired the damage.

Sources indicate that the Kerch Strait Bridge’s future prospects look much bleaker now following the latest missile and drone strikes. The bridge was initially constructed in two years, and engineering experts told The Newly introduced York Times that repairs to the bridge roadway could also take two years under normal circumstances.

But they also agreed that any damage to the bridge’s piers could extend that repair time—and Russian repair efforts would likely be at risk from future Ukrainian missile and drone attacks.

This story was updated on November 19, 2026 with information about an additional Ukrainian strike on the Kerch Strait Bridge on the night between November 18 and November 19.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods.".

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar noted, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Industry observers note that climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

Recent findings suggest that while using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

In a recent development, "Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar mentioned. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute remarked it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky matter. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way.".

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

In a recent development, "You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming.".

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar mentioned, describing them as a potential "breakthrough.".

Industry observers note that carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

Sources indicate that "Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar mentioned.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an crucial source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

Industry observers note that the balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person noted, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have noted.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it notes is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the upcoming intelligence.

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

According to recent reports, still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

Ted Cruz-led committee approves Trump FCC nominee 15-0 as Democrats boycott vote

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.
  • It has been revealed that all 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent.
  • It has been revealed that nominees are vetted in committees first, and then require majority approval from the Senate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote.

It has been revealed that all 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz noted at today’s hearing.

It has been revealed that nominees are vetted in committees first, and then require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.

Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz noted Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.”.

According to recent reports, technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. Until today.”.

At a hearing last week, Thumann remarked she never worked with Carr on media-related topics, leading to accusations that she provided false testimony. “I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related complications,” Thumann said after Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked, “Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?”.

“It appears that Ms. Thumann misled the Committee and offered false testimony, seriously calling into question her judgment and character and impeding the Committee’s work in determining whether she should be seated on the Commission,” Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz yesterday. “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media-related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount.”.

According to recent reports, the FCC website describes Thumann as senior counsel to Carr on matters before the Wireline Bureau, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, and the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. Emails obtained in a public records request by the group Protect Democracy show she had some involvement in media-related matters.

In a recent development, thumann provided follow-up responses to senators’ questions this week. She said that her work sometimes includes “reviewing documents or filings in a matter outside of my designated portfolio. However, I did not have any conversations with Paramount, CBS, or Skydance related to the merger.”.

Thumann has been referred to as Thumann Severs in the nomination process, but she uses the name Thumann.

Luján wrote that Thumann “played a role in processing informal complaints related to” alleged news distortion on CBS’s 60 Minutes, and that “she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” However, Thumann was only a recipient of the Kimmel-related emails we found in a search of the messages.

The emails do show that Thumann approved language used in a response the FCC gave to complaints about the alleged news distortion in a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. The response informed people who submitted complaints that they should instead submit comments on an FCC docket that had been set up for the 60 Minutes proceeding.

According to recent reports, “Hi Kristi, I have confirmed with the Chairman and Erin that we would like for complainants to be encouraged to resubmit their news distortion complaints in the relevant ECFS [Electronic Comment Filing System] proceeding,” Thumann wrote. “Can you please work on some draft language to send to consumers that would advise them on this step (including how to use ECFS)?”.

In a recent development, democrats revealed yesterday that they would try to prevent a quorum for today’s vote. They objected to adding a third Republican to the committee while a Democratic seat remains empty.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Cantwell noted in a statement.

Cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members remarked.

Recent findings suggest that cruz noted today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session.

Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today.

In the Standing Rules of the Senate, paragraph 7 of rule XXVI says that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.”.

While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson said this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.”.

FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz said that’s not a requirement.

“There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz stated during the Republican-only meeting.

The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It states, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”.

According to recent reports, republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term.

It has been revealed that “There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

Community backlash to a datacentre expansion in inner Melbourne that resulted in NextDC’s share price dropping 40% will change the way the organization engages with communities – and it says it will no longer pursue new developments near homes.

The company held its first annual general meeting since it was forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in West Footscray after power provider Jemena paused construction of new 22-metre power poles amid community protest.

The share price has since recovered to over $9 a share, but not before rival Goodman Group bought a nearly 10% stake in the business.

Shareholders revolted against the company at the AGM, issuing a second strike against executive pay, but the resulting motion on whether to spill the board was resoundingly defeated on Friday.

The chief executive, Craig Scroggie, noted it was his “hardest AGM” in 15 years, and that he ultimately took responsibility for “delivery, power, planning, approvals, construction and community support”.

“At M3, we needed to work more closely with our power and construction partners, and with the community,” he mentioned. “We are now doing that.”.

Scroggie said the community deserved to be heard earlier than they had been during the Jemena construction works, and it was NextDC’s job to do that.

“M3 has certainly changed how we plan, build and operate alongside our neighbours,” he mentioned.

According to recent reports, “For more than 15 years we’ve built datacentres right across the country, and what earned trust then is not enough now. Community expectations have moved in the age of artificial intelligence and we must move with them.”.

In addition to a new community consultative committee, including a standing forum for residents and local stakeholders, NextDC has stated it will have a dedicated project website and contact channels with defined response times for complaints and inquiries.

NextDC’s chair, Doug Flynn, also revealed that the company would change where it builds in future.

“Given community sensitivities, we do not intend to pursue fresh development opportunities that are near residential properties,” Flynn remarked.

“The pushback against datacentres is very different right now than it was … six or so years ago.”.

Flynn said that the M3 site in inner Melbourne had been an industrial site for 100 years, and had petrochemical works on it before NextDC built the datacentre.

After the blowback to taller power poles led to a delayed expansion, Flynn stated the Jemena employee overseeing community engagement left the business.

It has been revealed that “They recognise that they were just charging ahead regardless of community,” he remarked. “And they got a bloody nose.

“Unfortunately, we did as well.”.

A spokesperson for Jemena declined to comment, but pointed to a September statement announcing its general manager for electricity networks had decided to step down.

Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult.".

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and stated that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, mentioned Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Industry observers note that local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

Industry observers note that "Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

According to recent reports, kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he remarked, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

In a recent development, yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and mentioned the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," noted Popovych.

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff declared that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers at the moment at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

Superhuman pushes its Go assistant everywhere

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products.
  • Industry observers note that while some of the manufacturer’s AI features have faced criticism, Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year.
  • The assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly — and also manages other agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assistant, making agents available in Docs, and third-party agent integrations.

Industry observers note that while some of the manufacturer’s AI features have faced criticism, Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year. With the new rollout, it is making Go learn context across different apps and give better personalized suggestions for prompts. Superhuman is revamping its onboarding flow to let customers connect their preferred tools and load context about their work upfront.

The assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly — and also manages other agents. Superhuman is also making the agent proactive, which means it looks for your schedule, keeps an eye on your email, and even drafts responses. The updated Go agent also learns people’ writing styles and responds accordingly in email and Docs.

The productivity tech giant is adding 20 fresh connected agents, including DeepL, Legora, Amplitude, Databricks, and Blackboard, through its Go SDK.

The tech giant is also thinking about adding AI to different products, including Docs and Superhuman Mail. In Docs, all Go agents work natively, and you can set them off to work on different tasks in the background. Users can also set routines to trigger workflows based on events.

Industry observers note that until now, Mail has used AI as its central tool, which is being replaced by Go. Customers can also do enterprise search by using data from the tech giant knowledge base and connected tools. Go also uses this context to form drafts and organize the inbox across Google and Outlook accounts.

Superhuman acquired notetaker Fathom in September to add more context to its suite. The tech giant is now rolling out live collaborative notetaking, which would be shared across the team. Plus, Go can now make decisions post-meeting, like forming an initial draft of a proposal.

According to recent reports, the company’s CEO, Shishir Mehrotra, said that Go has had good momentum with over 1 million active customers. There are a host of agents now that are vying for users’ attention on both the personal and professional front. Mehrotra thinks that while Go is more work-focused, it can help with personal emails and schedules.

In a recent development, “One of the reasons why these assistants have been popular is that they treat you as a whole person and recognize that we need to cover both extremes. Go is definitely more work-focused than some of the tools coming out of the pure consumer ecosystem. It doesn’t mean we draw the boundary at helping you with your personal tasks or helping you with your calendar or all of your email,” he told TechCrunch over a call.

While Go might not directly compete with the likes of Instinct, Muse, and Fo, Superhuman wants users to choose its assistant over something like OpenAI’s Dots or Claude Duet.
