📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in February 2024.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.

Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his fresh partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.

The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

On Friday, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC went through Lamarre-Condon’s attempts to clean up the alleged crime scene and dispose of the bodies as the trial wrapped up its ninth week.

The defence does not dispute Lamarre-Condon’s actions in the aftermath of the deaths, instead arguing he did so because he “panicked considerably”.

But Hatfield told the New South Wales supreme court his conduct was not that of a person who panicked after something unintended, but behaviour that was “deliberate, sustained and very purposeful”.

The crown prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took extensive steps to distance himself from the deaths, manufactured evidence to make it look like Baird was alive by texting people from the dead man’s phone, and “disposed of the bodies in an utterly callous manner”.

“The lies, concealment and disposal of the bodies are not equally explained by manslaughter or accident,” Hatfield mentioned.

“His conduct is immediate and the steps are so extreme you might think it’s only consistent with having intentionally killed both men and a planned murder.

“His explanations in his evidence … ring completely hollow.”.

Lamarre-Condon claimed his initial steps came out of concern for the housemates, but by leaving the bodies in the courtyard, he risked them making a “completely terrifying discovery”, Hatfield told the court.

Hatfield said the accused had an understanding that “exactly what he’d done was murder”.

“His conduct was an exercise in avoiding accountability in what he knew he had done,” he remarked.

Earlier on Friday, Hatfield re-iterated the prosecution’s arguments about the day of the alleged murders, playing the audio of the two gunshots that killed Baird.

The lawyer invited the jury to consider what they could do in the four seconds between the shots.

Making a gun gesture with his own hand, Hatfield argued there was only time to walk a few steps and fire and “not opportunity for much more than that”.

Lamarre-Condon then came up with a “pathetic moral dilemma” and claimed he feared he could be killed in jail, when he knew he would be in protective custody, the prosecution alleged.

His decisions to go to Sushi Train for dinner with his friend and undergo a minor elective surgery in the aftermath of the alleged murders showed Lamarre-Condon was calm and at points “completely relaxed”, Hatfield alleged.

But within days, the accused must have been “feeling the world closing in”, the prosecutor mentioned.

“He wants credit for handing himself in to police … but even in his last hours he’s there going to Bunnings, buying paint and painting the inside of the van … still trying to cover up what happened,” Hatfield told the court.

Lamarre-Condon eventually helped police locate the bodies, but only after being told about the state’s no body, no parole laws.

“The bodies were left … for a further four days after he’s arrested,” Hatfield mentioned. “Evidence all the while being destroyed.

“Imagine the grief [of the families] on those four days.”.

The defence alleges Baird and Davies were killed in two separate struggles when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”.

Going through forensic evidence, Hatfield noted Davies’ DNA was found on the gun, but says this is “entirely unremarkable evidence”, alleging Lamarre-Condon had handled his body at the scene and then touched the weapon.

“It’s just something he’s grabbed on to in order to weave this invented narrative about Mr Davies shooting himself,” the lawyer noted.

Earlier evidence provided by a weapons expert indicated it would take the force equivalent to almost 3kg to pull the trigger, which would not happen without a conscious movement on behalf of the person holding the gun, the prosecution alleged.

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vladimir Putin spoke at a press conference following a historic summit with Xi Jinping and Donald Trump.

Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.

In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.

A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.

But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin remarked Moscow's response would be even more significant.

Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.

Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles.

From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplied its troops in southern Ukraine.

It has been revealed that commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors.".

The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.

The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.

It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.

Sources indicate that thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.

Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.

President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Recent findings suggest that the seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.

Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack earlier this week.

In response to Tuesday's hit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

But the operation to repair it could take a long time, and it will likely have to be carried out under frequent Ukrainian fire.

Russia has regularly targeted Ukrainian civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.

This week alone, as the Crimean Bridge was being hit, Moscow targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Nimble enters the item-tracking market with eco-friendly luggage tags and keychains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category.
  • Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based company announced Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.
  • Nimble’s upcoming collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category. The latest entrant is Nimble, the sustainable accessories brand best known for its charging products.

Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based company announced Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.

Nimble’s upcoming collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up. Apple’s AirTag helped popularize the category, while Google recently introduced its first-party tracker, the $29 Pixel Tag, powered by its Find Hub network. Meanwhile, established third-party players, such as Chipolo and Pebblebee, continue to expand their lineups.

Nimble is taking a slightly different approach. Rather than introducing another stand-alone tracker to attach to a set of keys or slip into a bag, the company has integrated tracking technology directly into practical accessories, including wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers.

The lineup includes seven products, ranging from the $14.95 Trace Tag, which features a replaceable coin-cell battery, to the $49.95 Trace Folio, a passport cover with built-in rechargeable tracking. Other options include the Trace Keyfob ($19.95), Trace Slim Wallet Card ($29.95), Trace Keychain ($29.95), Trace Luggage Tag ($39.95), and Trace Wallet ($39.95).

The entire collection is compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub networks.

Ross Howe, co-founder and CEO of Nimble, told us that the company’s approach is designed to differentiate its products from traditional trackers.

“Most locators are built as utility gadgets, not as things you want to own. Few were asking why the locator couldn’t just be the nice object itself. So, for example, we made a wallet findable instead of making a tracker that fits a wallet. We also thought more options should be rechargeable.”.

The Trace Luggage Tag and Trace Folio are arguably the most interesting products in the collection. Dedicated luggage tags and passport covers with built-in tracking remain relatively uncommon, giving Nimble an opportunity to stand out in a market. There are only a few alternatives, including Spotminder’s $59 passport cover with Apple Find My support, which is $10 more than Nimble’s option. Knog Scout offers a luggage tag, although I find its design a little too bulky.

In a recent development, rechargeability is another appealing aspect of Nimble’s new collection. Several models support USB-C or wireless charging, offering an alternative to the disposable batteries found in many traditional trackers. Howe says battery life lasts for “months,” with the Trace Keyfob, for example, rated for approximately six months on a charge.

Sustainability is another major part of Nimble’s pitch. Staying true to its roots, the tech giant has incorporated eco-friendly materials throughout the collection, including recycled plastics and plant-based, vegan aloe leather. The products have also undergone third-party testing for chemicals of concern.

“We’ve spent the last two years going through the chemistry of our products line by line to remove or limit as many harmful ingredients as possible. Trace is the first collection designed specifically to meet these higher standards. We’re not 100% yet, but the independent labs checking our work will help us get there,” Howe stated.

In a recent development, the collection is available now through its website and Amazon. All seven products come in five color options: Black, Stone, Tangerine, Plum, and Teal.

#157. Tech Report: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage

Tech Report: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
  • In a recent development, across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade.
  • It has been revealed that yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

In a recent development, across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

It has been revealed that yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”.

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

Industry observers note that as the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory states he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”.

Industry observers note that given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most significant outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” notes João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”.

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a substantial cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having problems, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.

It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech firm may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.

According to recent reports, another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with challenges. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.

It has been revealed that when a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying glitch. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts.

When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy upgrade, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.

Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she indicates.

Industry observers note that most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.

Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that promptly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.

Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the Internet infrastructure tech giant Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.

In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.

Industry observers note that if all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It’s going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”.

In a recent development, aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty enhancement, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved rapidly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé claims, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”.

In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.

In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?

For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through Internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don’t think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory states.

In a recent development, “If you’re immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don’t really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what’s different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”.

The cost of the US war in Iran, which Donald Trump launched without Congressional approval on February 28, blew past $48.3 billion (€44 billion) on November 13, according to Pentagon budgetary official Arthur Miller.

Miller laid out the figures during Thursday testimony before the US Senate Armed Services Committee as his nomination to become Navy comptroller is considered.

Miller said the costs cover US military operations, equipment and munitions but not damage sustained at US military installations across the Middle East.

According to news agency AP, damage to hundreds of aircraft hangars, barracks, radar systems, warehouses and other US military infrastructure has run up into the billions of dollars, however, Miller failed to provide an estimate of the total cost when pressed during the hearing.

Committee Chairman Roger Wicker, a Republican from Mississippi, called on Miller to provide the figures as soon as possible.

In October, the Wall Street Journal cited Pentagon sources who remarked damage to US facilities in the region could range from $5 billion to as much as $15 billion.

The Washington-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies put the cost for repairing buildings alone — excluding equipment and systems inside — at more than $4 billion.

Tech Report: The GTA 6 star system states a lot more than just your Wanted level

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that rockstar Games' first gameplay trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 from August suggested the developer had tinkered with some of the core mechanics of the series, including Wanted levels.
  • According to recent reports, some of this is thanks to the game's new concept of Heat, pieces of information the police learn about the player characters that can linger even after your Wanted level lowers.
  • Industry observers note that the most obvious visual difference between GTA 6 and GTA 5 is the reintroduction of a sixth Wanted level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rockstar Games' first gameplay trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 from August suggested the developer had tinkered with some of the core mechanics of the series, including Wanted levels. Now that GTA 6 is out, we have a much better sense of how much has actually changed. While your Wanted level has always been able to communicate a sense of how many police officers are looking for you and how intently they're looking, the updated system also bakes in a lot more detail about what police actively know about protagonists Jason and Lucia.

According to recent reports, some of this is thanks to the game's new concept of Heat, pieces of information the police learn about the player characters that can linger even after your Wanted level lowers. But the visual changes to the Wanted system's iconic star ratings convey nearly as much. Here's how Rockstar's approach to Wanted levels has changed in Grand Theft Auto VI.

Industry observers note that the most obvious visual difference between GTA 6 and GTA 5 is the reintroduction of a sixth Wanted level. In the last Grand Theft Auto, your Wanted level maxed out at five stars. As Rockstar teased during its gameplay trailer, GTA 6 caps out at six stars. This is a return to the rating system of older games, going as far back as Grand Theft Auto III — or even further if you consider the "police heads" top-down GTA games used to communicate police response.

Sources indicate that as in past games, the number of stars lets you know how hard the police are looking for you. One star could just be a few cops tailing you, while a full six stars indicates a dramatic, militarized response. Besides being a throwback, opting for six stars seems like it allows Rockstar to offer some nuance and variety to the series' classic chase experience. You might eventually get bored if every bank robbery devolves into a helicopter chase.

Just committing a robbery doesn't necessarily mean your Wanted level will rise, either. According to IGN's hands-on demo and interview with Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson, crimes need to actually be reported to police to provoke a response. "The Wanted system in GTA 6 requires that someone witness the crime, or an alarm needs to be set off for it to be reported to the law," Nelson told IGN. "Our dispatch is extremely specific in what it knows.".

Once you are "wanted" for a crime, GTA 6 offers a lot more visual information to tell you what police right now know and nudge you toward escaping their scrutiny. Those include icons for the different kinds of information the police know about you as part of the Heat system, and also different treatments of your Wanted level star rating.

Industry observers note that when police have direct line of sight with you, your stars are solid white, according to GameSpot, and only start flashing white once you've broken line of sight. Meanwhile, your stars turn red when you're near a crime scene but the police don't know where you are or hollow white when the police are looking for you but have no idea what you look like.

Industry observers note that at the same time, some information about the police is also obstructed. GameSpot reports you won't be able to see the police on your minimap, which makes it harder to blueprint escape routes in advance. It also says once you do reach a six-star Wanted level, you'll be pursued throughout the game map, making clean exits more difficult. All of these changes seem like they'll make the fundamental cops-and-robbers gameplay of Grand Theft Auto 6 more engaging. Or at the very least, different from what people have come to expect from the series.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former opposition leader warns party against being ‘One Nation lite’ as he becomes eighth out of 24 Liberal MPs not to recontest seat in March.

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

The New South Wales opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, notes she is “pretty sure” the exodus of Liberals before the March state election has finished, after Mark Speakman became the eighth MP to decide not to recontest their lower house seats.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly before the vote, Speakman said he would not run again in his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

A third of the 24 current Liberal MPs have announced they will not recontest their seat in March, including Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Alister Henskens and Mark Taylor.

In a press conference on Friday, Sloane insisted the departures were not an indictment of the party’s election prospects.

Recent findings suggest that “No, that’s not the truth. What we are seeing is an impressive cross section of abilities and talent and tenure in our party,” she told reporters in the same room where, exactly a year ago, Speakman declared he would resign as Liberal leader in her favour.

It has been revealed that “We have people who have been in government before. We have people who have been in for a medium amount of time, and we’re going to have people with fresh ideas.”.

Sloane remarked she had tried to convince Speakman to stay and said many of the MPs leaving had been in parliament for more than 10 years, although Lane is a first-term MP.

Sloane noted a significant number of Liberals had retired before the 2023 election, in which the Coalition lost government and the party dropped nine seats.

According to recent reports, asked if she could guarantee that further MPs would not step down ahead of the March vote, Sloane stated: “Look, I certainly hope not. I certainly hope not. I’m pretty sure that’s done. I’m pretty sure that’s done.”.

Since last year’s leadership spill, the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in NSW to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.

Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is now at 26%.

Last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.

On Friday, Sloane rejected the claims from “anonymous names in a Financial Review article”, saying the Coalition only needed to flip six Labor seats to form minority government.

In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, said the Liberals were “said to face an existential threat” following a wipeout at the 2025 federal election and an “orange wave that seems to be coming across the country”.

He warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.

Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman remarked Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.

“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he noted.

“I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”.

Speakman, a barrister, served as environment minister between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.

He was chosen as the Liberal and opposition leader after Dominic Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.

On Thursday, he remarked being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and, while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.

He mentioned his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.

Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, confirmed the former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.

On Friday, Sloane noted Raffoul had been talking to her about Liberal party roles “only two months ago”.

“She’s decided to chase personal ambition. She’s a very ambitious person, but she’s changed sides, and that’s a decision Chris Minns has made.”.

Earlier, the NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, rejected the idea that One Nation was pushing Labor to become “Liberal lite”, saying Raffoul’s candidacy reflected “a journey that I think many Liberal people are going through as well”.

#151. Anthropic’s IPO puts AI’s circular financing boom to the test

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1124 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Anthropic’s IPO puts AI’s circular financing boom to the test

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that arriving at public markets today, Anthropic’s IPO is poised to raise billions for the organization and its investors.
  • It has been revealed that amazon and Google, two of Anthropic’s largest infrastructure partners, hold stakes valued around a combined $307.9 billion at the firm’s updated IPO price of $83 per share.
  • A handful of other AI infrastructure providers are also positioned to benefit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that arriving at public markets today, Anthropic’s IPO is poised to raise billions for the organization and its investors. But the biggest surprise may be just how much of that money will end up going to supplier-investors.

It has been revealed that amazon and Google, two of Anthropic’s largest infrastructure partners, hold stakes valued around a combined $307.9 billion at the firm’s updated IPO price of $83 per share. Amazon, which invested $18 billion into the AI startup, would see its 14.7% stake hit upwards of $159 billion, while Google’s 13.7% stake is valued at nearly $149 billion, according to share ownership figures disclosed in Anthropic’s IPO prospectus.

A handful of other AI infrastructure providers are also positioned to benefit. Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft, Broadcom, Micron, and TSMC have joined Google in committing $26 billion to Anthropic at its IPO price in a private placement.

It has been revealed that in total, Google has invested $12.3 billion into Anthropic since 2023, with another promised $30 billion dependent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. And with the exception of TSMC, Anthropic has unveiled multibillion-dollar strategic partnerships with its other infrastructure supplier investors — including Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Microsoft, and Micron — that would see Anthropic purchasing their products.

Recent findings suggest that this is the circular financing that has made some observers so skeptical of the AI boom. These companies are not just investors; they’re also Anthropic’s biggest suppliers. It might look like Amazon and Google are putting billions into Anthropic, but they get that money right back when Anthropic needs to train a model or serve Claude to users. From afar, it looks like unprecedented revenue growth for cloud companies and unprecedented fundraising from Anthropic — but it’s just the same money passing from one pocket to another.

Today’s IPO marks a critical change in that financing system, the moment it might just become self-sustaining. Those investments appear to have paid off, and are now liquid. Anthropic is still operating at a net loss of tens of billions of dollars each quarter — but it will no longer be suppliers and private investors footing the bill. Now, capital will come from a mix of public-market investors and corporate bonds, neither of which have the conflicts-of-interest that caused concerns before.

And critically, the organization’s new bottom line looks pretty good.

Once it debuts, Anthropic is expected to have about $220 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, including proceeds from its IPO and the $26 billion private placement. Anthropic also has the ability to pay for future commitments in stock.

Joey Brookhart, who leads the Tokenomics team at SemiAnalysis, estimates that Anthropic needs roughly $280 billion in cumulative revenue over the next four years to pay for its compute bill, which Brookhart said is “achievable given where they will be next year from a revenue perspective.”.

“The ownership stake is very worthwhile, and those companies no longer need any more support from [suppliers],” Brookhart told TechCrunch. “Amazon doesn’t need to prop them up anymore. The revenue is all coming from other customers.”.

Sources indicate that that doesn’t mean the server bills are going down, though. Anthropic has already committed to spend $900 billion, primarily for compute and infrastructure, according to a regulatory filing. Certain agreements have termination provisions, but Brookhart thinks the tech giant is in a strong position to pay up.

On the other side, Anthropic generated $17 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue, putting the company on pace for a $68 billion annualized rate for the year. If Anthropic continues to grow at its current trajectory, Brookhart believes it could easily cover the gap needed to fund its compute.

Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, agreed.

According to recent reports, “By the time the IPO is done, Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any manufacturer has ever had,” Luria told TechCrunch, noting that the firm raised around $141 billion in capital and will take home around $91.7 billion in net proceeds at $83 per share. “And they’re not burning cash. They’re just going to have a war chest.”.

Industry observers note that A public listing will make Anthropic a more credible borrower, making it easier to raise money outside of public markets, notes Brookhart. That’s despite recent reports that creditors might not see Anthropic as “investment-grade” material.

According to recent reports, luria distinguished between Anthropic’s supplier investments and neoclouds like CoreWeave, which he sees as more purely supported by circular financing. “CoreWeave wouldn’t exist if Nvidia didn’t prop them up, and it probably won’t exist if Nvidia doesn’t bail them out,” Luria said.

Brookhart also pushed back on describing Anthropic’s financing as purely circular, saying it was still “additive to the ecosystem.”.

For both analysts, the biggest risk to Anthropic is simply that it will lose the AI race. Right now, the company’s growth is fueled by its status at the frontier of generative AI — but if it’s overtaken by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or even cheap open-weight models, that could change fast. As Luria put it: “If we’re all using other people’s models, then Anthropic’s not worth a trillion and a half dollars. It’s worth nothing.”.

According to recent reports, but regardless of who wins the frontier, compute suppliers will likely be just fine. Neither Brookhart nor Luria believe Anthropic’s growth is at risk, despite some arguments that cheaper tokens and more competition will directly affect the AI manufacturer’s bottom line.

“For Amazon and Google, the risk isn’t actually that high because in that scenario, we’re using other models,” Luria remarked. “I’m arguing we’re going to use a lot more AI. I don’t know if it’s all Anthropic’s AI…. That’s still going to come from a data center managed by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat mentioned to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.
  • Sources indicate that four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far.
  • In a recent development, personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The damaged boat washed ashore on a beach.

Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat mentioned to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.

Sources indicate that four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far. Dozens of people are still missing.

In a recent development, personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.

This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.

Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).

"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.

A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.

However, a local official told Reuters news agency it was carrying 50 people, adding that the boat hit a rock as migrants were transferring from small fishing boats to a larger vessel.

Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.

He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.

Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.

Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.

The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.

It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.

The Senegalese navy said it had rescued more than 1,400 people on Monday and Tuesday this week.

As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.

They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.

Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.

They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.

On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.

In a recent development, it remarked more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

#147. Breaking: NASA's upcoming Moon looks have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (993 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: NASA's upcoming Moon looks have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA recently confirmed a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.
  • In a recent development, the moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon.
  • Sources indicate that these changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA recently confirmed a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.

In a recent development, the moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit.

Sources indicate that these changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.

In a recent development, for Starship, the evolved initiative has SpaceX fueling a Starship lunar lander in low-Earth orbit before docking with Orion in high-Earth orbit. The crew will fly to the Moon on board Orion before two of the four astronauts transfer into Starship for a landing on the Moon.

Due to the docking configuration with Starship, Orion must now fly backward to the Moon, with its Service Module at the top of the stack. This is a fundamentally different flying posture than Orion was designed for, Shireman said, and creates problems for Orion’s propulsion system.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, the Service Module, which is provided by the European Space Agency, will require modifications to its propellant tanks. This is because liquid propellant would move toward the gas inlet side of the tanks, rather than settling in the direction expected during normal operation.

In a recent development, “When you push it the other way, the liquid goes to the gas end of the tank, and you don’t want the liquid in the gas part,” Shireman noted. “Bad things can happen to you.” To address this, he said, the European Space Agency and its main contractor, Airbus, are modifying the vehicle’s tanks for Starship lunar missions.

Industry observers note that NASA and Lockheed engineers have also been studying the impact of increased acceleration on Orion when the vehicle is attached to Starship. Under Orion’s original mission architecture, the spacecraft would experience accelerations of about 0.1 to 0.15 g during the translunar injection burn, Shireman said. But with Starship providing the thrust, the acceleration would increase to approximately 0.8 to 1 g, acting in the opposite direction from the one originally planned.

Orion’s structure must be certified to handle a substantially higher acceleration in the opposite direction, Shireman remarked.

Industry observers note that before astronauts land on the Moon, NASA is also planning a mission in low-Earth orbit to test Orion’s interactions with the lunar landers. Shireman mentioned this change in looks for Artemis III, revealed earlier this year, has created latest hazards, as Orion was not designed to spend more than a short period of time in low-Earth orbit.

Sources indicate that heating is a concern, he said, because Orion was designed for deep space, which is colder than the thermal environment closer to Earth. For example, he said, Orion has passive thermal features designed to prevent the spacecraft from getting too cold in deep space. One of these is a silver-looking exterior tape that dissipates electrical charge and limits the radiation of heat into space. As a result, some of this tape will be removed for the Artemis III mission.

Engineers are also analyzing how to manage electrical loads to reduce heating and protect the avionics and crew cabin.

Recent findings suggest that another major change that stems from spending approximately two weeks in low-Earth orbit is the orbital debris environment, which is more congested than in deep space. Shireman said NASA and Lockheed have not completed their assessment of the orbital-debris risk associated with the new mission profile. This should be done by January, and, if the risks are too high, it might lead to modifications of Orion’s orbit for the mission.

“There’s going to be a higher risk from an MMOD standpoint,” Shireman mentioned of orbital debris near Earth. “It’ll be higher risk than flying out to the Moon.”.

Earlier this year, NASA removed the lunar landing from Artemis III, turning the mission into a demonstration of rendezvous and docking operations in low-Earth orbit. The agency is now targeting 2027 for the mission, leaving Orion and the lunar landing companies with a compressed schedule to complete substantial technical integration work.

This may seem like a fairly straightforward process, but docking is rather complex. It involves mechanical capabilities like hooks, connectors, and pins; there are thruster-plume interactions with the landers, including possible damage from hot or abrasive exhaust; concerns about whether Orion’s laser system might incorrectly interpret reflections from surfaces on Starship or Blue Moon; and more.

According to recent reports, “We were going to do that work, but not on Artemis III, and not for both of the landers,” Shireman stated of docking with Starship and Blue Moon. “It was going to be spaced out, so all that work gets crunched into this time frame.”.

Lockheed is working closely with NASA to prepare Orion to maintain an Artemis III schedule for a launch in summer or fall of 2027.

“We’re working three shifts,” Shireman noted. “We had a zero-margin schedule already, so we’re, I call it hand-to-hand combat. Literally every day we’re clawing to see, ‘Hey, can we save a shift here? Can we save half a shift there?’”.

It has been revealed that shireman said he supports the urgency of Isaacman and NASA in their contest with China over the Moon. But it is important to keep an eye on mission safety, said Shireman, who worked at NASA during both the Challenger and Columbia accidents.

“We also have a responsibility to not go too fast and cut too many corners and make sure that we are not taking undue risks,” he mentioned.

  • The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information.

The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret.

The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.

The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort, arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.

Sources indicate that california-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.

Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. When reached for comment, Apple told TechCrunch that it welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.

Apple previously remarked that it has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”.

A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.

Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.

A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rose was a 17-time Major League Baseball All-Star, but his legacy was tarnished by a lifetime ban.

US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.

"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that rose, who died in 2024 at the age of 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns. He was also given a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball (MLB) after an investigation revealed he bet on games.

The baseball star was posthumously reinstated to MLB, in which he played for 24 seasons, last year and made eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.

Trump also stated on Thursday that Rose's "record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken".

Recent findings suggest that in fact, Rose accumulated a record 4,256 hits - which MLB defines as a batter striking the baseball into fair territory and reaching base without doing so via an error or a fielder's choice - during his career, which is more than any other player. He played a total of 3,562 games.

It has been revealed that according to Trump, Rose "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess".

The US Constitution gives a sitting president the broad power to grant a pardon, which represents legal forgiveness and ends any further punishment.

Industry observers note that because Rose's pardon was issued after his death, it is largely symbolic and does not change Rose's Hall of Fame status. The Department of Justice (DoJ) typically does not process posthumous pardon applications, though presidents have still issued them.

The BBC has contacted the Hall of Fame and the DoJ for comment.

The US president had previously floated the idea of pardoning Rose in March last year before the MLB reinstated him.

"Major League Baseball didn't have the courage or decency to put the late, great, Pete Rose, also known as 'Charlie Hustle,' into the Baseball Hall of fame," he wrote on Truth Social at the time.

It has been revealed that "Now he is dead, will never experience the thrill of being selected, even though he was a FAR BETTER PLAYER than most of those who made it, and can only be named posthumously. WHAT A SHAME," Trump added.

MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred issued a decision in May 2025 that created a pathway for Rose to be eligible to be inducted into the baseball Hall of Fame - a ruling that also applied to 16 other people - as early as 2028.

In August 1989, Rose agreed to the permanent ban from the sport after MLB investigators found that he bet on his team, the Cincinnati Reds, multiple times while he was playing on and managing the team from 1985 to 1987.

In a recent development, in July 1990, after Rose admitted to failing to report $354,968 (Â£271,107) in income over a four-year period, he was sentenced to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform community service at the time.

Major League Baseball legend Rose dies aged 83.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.

Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.

The inquest in Lismore has heard women chose free or home births for reasons including traumatic experiences, a lack of trust in clinicians, and a lack of services.

Recent findings suggest that baby DH died about eight hours after he was born in a free birth – with a doula but no medical professionals present. The court earlier heard he turned purple, was struggling to breathe and had became floppy.

His parents gave evidence they were worried but the doula kept reassuring them their baby was OK, then left.

The doula denied many of their claims, and denied that she gave them any clinical advice.

Expert neonatologist and associate professor Nicholas Evans mentioned on Friday that Baby DH’s complex heart abnormalities “would have been readily detectable” in a routine pregnancy scan after which he would have been referred to a paediatric cardiologist.

It was a “missed opportunity”, he told the court.

Paediatric cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks mentioned it was “highly likely” all the abnormalities would have been identified in a routine scan before birth.

Even if the extent of the abnormalities wasn’t clear, he told the court, the scan would have shown the baby needed to be born at a major hospital with cardiac surgery capabilities.

“The site of [Baby DH’s] birth meant that he didn’t have a chance.”.

Baby D’s mother did not know she was having twins, and at first thought she’d delivered Baby D’s placenta, only to realise it was a stillborn second twin.

Experts at the inquest agreed it was impossible to know exactly why Baby D died. They discussed the possibility it was because self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali did not clamp the umbilical cord before cutting it, but Evans told the court that it was ultimately most likely from respiratory distress because of his compromised heart function.

Baby D might have survived if someone who could do advanced resuscitation had arrived in under 10 minutes, he said, but the “root cause” was that it was not known the mother was carrying twins before the births.

“If [twins] had been diagnosed, at 18 weeks, as it would usually in pregnancy, there would have been very close monitoring.”.

Recent findings suggest that baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.

The mother had been for an ultrasound at 12 weeks, which had put the date of birth at 28 July, 2020.

But the mother distrusted hospitals and trusted Kali, her birth keeper, the court previously heard.

Kali told her to calculate her due date from the date of conception, an unreliable measure that put the date of birth in mid-August.

That recalculation, Evans wrote in his report to the court, was the “root cause” of the glitch.

“The standard practice now is that you don’t allow a pregnancy to go beyond 42 completed weeks,” Evans said on Friday.

Expert midwives earlier told the court they didn’t have statistics for babies born beyond 43 weeks because it was so rare.

A 19 August ultrasound highlighted the pregnancy had become a medical emergency – but Kali advised her to “go home and rest”. It is “more likely than not” that the baby would have survived had she gone to hospital after the ultrasound, Evans mentioned.

Baby B’s mother was warned multiple times she needed to go to hospital to give birth to her twins, but she was determined to have a home birth. Rather than let her have a free birth, four midwives assisted her and the head midwife repeatedly counselled her about the risks.

The mother declined ultrasounds as well as a test for early onset group B streptococcus (GBS) – an organism present in 15 to 20% of women that infects the babies of about 2% of carriers.

Baby B likely died of GBS, pneumonia and sepsis, Evans told the court on Friday, while his twin fell ill but survived. Many infected babies survive in hospital thanks to antibiotics, he added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday in the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing AI responsibly. In his speech ahead of the Nasdaq opening bell, Amodei vowed that the AI company would not bend to either business or political pressure and would “remain under human control.”.

Reading the speech from a printout, the CEO began by talking about Anthropic’s origins as a way to build powerful technology to help humanity — something that he stated was inspired by the loss of his father to a disease that became curable just a few years later.

Recent findings suggest that he acknowledged that while human intelligence had made diseases like the plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world, there were still too few scientists with too little time to make progress in other areas of disease. AI, he remarked, could help with this by working in concert with humans to further medical progress.

Sources indicate that it’s telling that Amodei began with a story highlighting AI’s potentially lifesaving applications, since he’s warned repeatedly about the risks of advancing the technology too promptly. In September, Amodei drew headlines when he outlined a blueprint to pace AI development, which included things like coordinating with other leading companies on safety standards and embedding evaluators from third-party organizations to verify that companies were following their safety commitments.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, and xAI owner Elon Musk stated they agreed with Amodei’s position, although few concrete commitments have been made.

Sources indicate that in this morning’s speech, Amodei again stressed the need to progress AI technology and the safety required in doing so. He referred to the “very real risks” of AI in the hands of bad actors, whether those were individuals or nation-states, and the potential for things like “economic disruption” and “losing control of AI systems.”.

Anthropic believes these risks are avoidable, he noted, as long as there are safeguards in place. Amodei stated the company would continue to be invested in the work of AI alignment and testing, and developing fresh ways to understand AI behavior so it could remain under human control.

It has been revealed that “There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us,” he said. “The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double and triple checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.”.

“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei concluded.

His sister, Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, echoed these sentiments in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, noting that while the risks were real, the promise of AI was also “incredible.”.

“We were really founded on this idea that it is our job to mitigate those risks, and I think we have to date done an incredible job doing that. We obviously have more work ahead of us, but we are deeply committed to safety,” she added. The full text of Dario Amodei’s opening speech is below:.

Thank you, Daniela. My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind. Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that just a few years later became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments. So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket — tools for gene editing, tools for gene synthesis, tools for controlling brain cells with light — started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking, from intelligence.

According to recent reports, human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades. It took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR. Nature is full of these patterns, but we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them. Too few scientists with too [little] time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would have taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

Industry observers note that I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point, all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time, and although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe these processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by a few years. Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many other applications of Claude. Our customers, the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people, are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth, lift people out of poverty, protect democracy and free societies, even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them, and I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

At the same time, we’ve always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or by nation-states to economic disruption to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable and we are building anyway, but because we think they are avoidable and we can avoid them. Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic’s DNA from the start, from safeguards against biological and cyber risks to alignment training and testing to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI and keeping it under human control. There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us, the incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.

It has been revealed that and to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control, we will not bend to either business nor political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing. If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.

Sources indicate that when the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which firm has the best models. Everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so. But the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better. Thank you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh collapsible sidebar in AI mode reveals your most recent searches.

Google is doubling down on Gemini AI in its desktop search, despite protestations from users and employees alike. The latest feature is a collapsible sidebar in AI mode that shows your most recent searches, in case you want to jump back to a previous query. "In testing, this sidebar made a substantial difference for making progress and continuing to explore the web," wrote VP of search Robby Stein on X.

The newly introduced sidebar is only available in Google Search's AI mode. Clicking anywhere on the left of the AI search window opens up the sidebar, showing all recent searches, both AI and organic. Then, selecting any of the sidebar descriptions opens up an AI mode search window on the subject. You can close the AI search sidebar at any time by clicking on the "close sidebar" icon at the top right.

Latest on the Google desktop homepage globally: we're rolling out a collapsible sidebar to easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches.

Recent findings suggest that people are coming to Search with more questions that aren't just one and done – and in testing, this sidebar made a significant difference for... pic.twitter.com/mKHz295tzK.

— Robby Stein (@rmstein) November 19, 2026.

Industry observers note that if you're like me and never use Google's dedicated AI Search mode, you won't see the new sidebar. Still, it's bound to ruffle some feathers among users and publishers who think there's already too much Gemini in Google Search. (As an, er, sidebar, I'd add that the feature would be nice to have in regular Search, as a list of recent queries would save me from having a zillion tabs open.).

Google seems to value its AI search development more than actual money, given that its market cap recently dropped by $500 billion after it admitted that AI search isn't earning as much as organic search. However, the company is likely focused on maintaining its AI search lead over rivals like ChatGPT and Claude. And, as CEO Sundar Pichai put it in the company's last earnings call, Google's commitment to AI is "long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise.".
